findings.statement: CXCR2 ranks first in the convergence ranking, with expression up in the meta-analysis (log2FC [gene=CXCR2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=2.838]), a high Open Targets genetic association component and a Phase 3 small-molecule antagonist (reparixin) plus several Phase 2 antagonists (navarixin, ladarixin, SX-682, danirixin, elubrixin). Open Targets lists these drugs in other indications, not as approved UC drugs.

CXCR2 has no cis-pQTL or gut eQTL instrument, so Mendelian randomisation did not test it (this is not evidence against it). Mouse support is literature only: many mouse colitis papers perturb CXCR2, including a selective antagonist that ameliorated acute colitis, but MGI has no single-gene colitis phenotype. Safety review shows no known safety events and no strong loss-of-function constraint. Reactome places it in neutrophil degranulation and chemokine receptor signalling; STRING links it with CXCL8, CXCL1 and CXCL5 at very high confidence.

CXCR1 is a close CXCR2 partner (shared antagonists reparixin, ladarixin, navarixin, SX-682) with expression up across cohorts and a moderate Open Targets genetic score; like CXCR2 it has no MR instrument, so human causal direction is untested.

CD274 (PD-L1) is the strongest genetically supported expression-led gene: higher plasma protein lowers UC risk (OR per SD [gene=CD274; type=mendelian_randomization; source=DATASET:MR_UKBPPP_UC; odds_ratio_per_sd=0.595]), it colocalises with the IBD GWAS signal and replicates in FinnGen and a second UC GWAS. Expression is raised in inflamed mucosa, so the biopsy increase looks compensatory, and PD-L1 blocking antibodies (approved in cancer) would act against the protective direction; this is a caution, not a drug candidate.

For CD274 the MR sensitivity checks show significant heterogeneity but no Egger intercept signal and correct Steiger direction; LOEUF is [gene=CD274; type=target_safety; source=DATASET:SAFETY; loeuf=0.476] (not strongly constrained) with no curated safety events. Mouse colitis literature is sparse and MGI has no phenotype. No gut eQTL was tested.

IL12B is an established UC target (top Open Targets association) and the leading plasma MR hit: higher protein raises UC risk (OR per SD [gene=IL12B; type=mendelian_randomization; source=DATASET:MR_UKBPPP_UC; odds_ratio_per_sd=1.539]), colocalises with IBD GWAS and replicates in FinnGen, so inhibition is the protective direction. This is a positive control showing the MR layer recovers known biology; it is not a new candidate.

CXCL5 is up in inflamed mucosa, yet genetically higher plasma CXCL5 lowers UC risk (OR per SD [gene=CXCL5; type=mendelian_randomization; source=DATASET:MR_UKBPPP_UC; odds_ratio_per_sd=0.634]) and replicates in FinnGen. Direction is opposite to what neutralising it would need, it relies on a tag variant and does not colocalise with IBD GWAS, so it is a biomarker of neutrophil recruitment rather than a clean target.

CXCL8 is among the most robustly up genes in all cohorts and has Phase 2 antibody drugs, but Open Targets genetic association is zero and plasma MR is null (p [gene=CXCL8; type=mendelian_randomization; source=DATASET:MR_UKBPPP_UC; p=0.289]), with no FinnGen replication. Its change is a strong activity or biomarker signal without human genetic support as a cause.

IDO1 is strongly up in all cohorts with an approved or late-stage inhibitor class in other indications, but neither plasma MR (p [gene=IDO1; type=mendelian_randomization; source=DATASET:MR_UKBPPP_UC; p=0.111]) nor colon eQTL MR is significant and Open Targets genetics is zero, so its increase is likely an interferon-response consequence rather than a driver.

SLC26A3 expression is decreased (lower) in inflamed mucosa across cohorts, with a moderate Open Targets genetic association and no approved or clinical drug in the tool output; the biopsy loss probably reflects depletion of mature absorptive epithelium.

In IBDverse gut cell-type eQTL MR (OLFM4+ crypt enterocyte progenitors), the UC risk allele is associated with the opposite sign of expression change to the biopsy loss, with OR per SD [gene=SLC26A3; type=mendelian_randomization_gut; source=DATASET:MR_GUT_EQTL_UC; layer=gut_cell; odds_ratio_per_sd=1.607]; it colocalises with the IBD GWAS signal and replicates in FinnGen. Genetic direction and biopsy change therefore disagree, and plasma MR was not tested.

JAK2 has a high Open Targets association and approved or clinical inhibitors, but is only modestly changed in biopsies (a genetically supported gene with a small expression shift) and has no MR instrument; JAK1, JAK3 and TYK2 appear among the known UC targets.

CHI3L1 is among the largest expression increases with replication in all cohorts and extensive literature, but has no Open Targets genetic association and no approved or clinical drug in the tool output; it fits a tissue biomarker, not a genetically supported target.

caveats: Convergence score rewards expression, replication and tractability; many top genes (CXCL8, IDO1, MMPs, S100A8/9, DUOX2) have zero Open Targets genetic association and are mostly activity biomarkers, not necessarily causes.
MR used plasma proteins or eQTL; many candidates (CXCR2, CXCR1, JAK2) have no instrument, which is not evidence against them.
Plasma protein is not mucosal protein; the only gut-layer result checked here was SLC26A3, and blood and gut layers were rarely both available.
Mouse evidence is literature counts only; MGI has no curated colitis phenotypes for the genes checked, and the literature check does not say the result direction.
Drugs listed are from Open Targets in any indication; none are asserted as UC-approved unless it is a known UC target.
Biopsy bulk expression may reflect infiltrating neutrophils and myeloid cells rather than epithelial change; not resolved here.
Not all top-40 genes were queried individually (about 40 tool-call budget).
